subject: computer-science
title: Cyber Security: Foundations
welcome_lead: Meet the threats and the shields that keep our data safe.
meta_desc: GCSE Computer Science adventure on cyber security threats and basic defences.
final_note: You now know the most common threats and how organisations defend against them.

concepts.def: Malicious software, including viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware, designed to damage systems or steal data.
Fraudulent emails or messages that imitate trusted organisations to trick users into revealing passwords, card numbers or other sensitive details.
An attack that tries many possible passwords or keys systematically until one works; longer, more complex passwords make it impractical.
Manipulating people, rather than technology, into giving away information or access, exploiting trust, fear or urgency.
Software or hardware that monitors traffic entering and leaving a network and blocks traffic that breaks the configured security rules.
Scrambling data using an algorithm and key so it is unreadable to anyone who intercepts it without the matching key.

walkthroughs.body_html:
• Malware: viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware
  • Phishing: fake emails impersonating banks or schools
  • Brute force: rapid password guessing
  • Social engineering: pretexting, baiting, tailgating

• Strong passwords + MFA
  • Firewalls filter traffic
  • Antivirus scans for malware
  • Encryption scrambles data
  • User training spots phishing
Urgent tone, generic greeting ('Dear customer'), spelling errors, mismatched URL on hover, asking for passwords. Real banks never email asking for full passwords.

mcqs.q: An email pretending to be from your bank, asking you to confirm your password, is an example of:
options: Phishing
Defragmentation
Compression
Overclocking
Systematically trying many possible passwords until one succeeds
Physically breaking the computer case
Cutting the network cables
Sending one polite request

mcqs.q: The role of a firewall is to:
options: Monitor and filter network traffic according to security rules
Speed up the processor
Back up files automatically
Clean the keyboard

mcqs.q: Which defence makes intercepted data unreadable to an attacker?
options: Encryption
A bigger monitor
Deleting cookies
Renaming files

mcqs.q: Does the padlock (HTTPS) icon mean a website is trustworthy?
options: Yes - phishing only works on passwords shorter than 8 characters.
Yes - the padlock proves the site's owners are honest.
No - it only means the connection is encrypted; criminals can obtain certificates too, so a phishing site can still show the padlock.
Yes - phishing sites cannot use HTTPS.

mcqs.q: Does a strong password protect you from phishing?
options: Yes - a long complex password cannot be phished.
Not by itself - phishing tricks you into handing the password over, so its strength is irrelevant; spotting fraudulent messages and using two-factor authentication help.
Yes - phishing only works on passwords shorter than 8 characters.
Yes - phishing sites cannot use HTTPS.

mcqs.q: Are phones and Macs immune to malware?
options: Yes - phishing sites cannot use HTTPS.
Yes - malware is only written for Windows PCs.
Yes - app stores make malware technically impossible.
No - any device running software can run malicious software; attackers target whatever platforms are popular, including mobile devices.
